parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: Can you walk me through your day-to-day responsibilities and what you need this service to do for you?

As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, deciding which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off each flight before it leaves. My legal responsibility is choosing the drone and the way it flies, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight who can also call it off. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I need the service to help me find out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
ASK technician: Can you walk me through your day-to-day responsibilities and what you need this service to do for you?

I keep the drones and charging equipment in working order for my company. My day involves adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send them to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
ASK desk: Can you walk me through your day-to-day responsibilities and what you need this service to do for you?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. Since a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, I need to manage this shared airspace information, which comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
